---
title: Computations
---

## Overview

A Quarto document can contain **executable cells**: fenced code blocks whose
info string is a language name wrapped in braces. Quarto hands each cell to
an [engine](engines.qmd), runs it, and splices the results into the rendered
document. For example, a cell written like this:

````markdown
```{r}
sum(1:10)
```
````

would, if run, produce `55` underneath it in the rendered page. (This page
only *shows* cells like this one — see the next section — so nothing on it
actually runs.)

## Rendering without running any code

`q2 render --no-execute` renders a document, or a whole project, without
executing any cell:

```bash
q2 render report.qmd --no-execute
```

Each cell is shown as code with no output, and no engine is started, so
this works on a machine without R, Python or Julia installed. Use it to
check a layout quickly, or to render a document whose cells are slow or
currently failing. A Jupyter notebook (`.ipynb`) still shows the outputs
stored in it; see [Notebooks](notebooks.qmd).

`--execute` is the default, and it means "execute as the documents ask".
It exists to cancel an earlier `--no-execute` on the same command line
(the last of the two wins).

::: callout-note
## Migrating from Quarto 1

In Quarto 1, `--execute` *forces* execution, overriding a document's
`execute: enabled: false`. In Quarto 2 it does not: a document that turns
execution off stays off. To execute such a document anyway, override its
metadata for the one render, with `-M 'execute:{enabled: true}'`.
:::

## Displaying code cells without running them

Writing *about* Quarto means showing readers what a cell looks like without
running it — for example, in a tutorial or in this documentation. The rule is
the ordinary Markdown one: **a fenced code block is displayed verbatim**, so a
cell written inside one is shown, not executed.

To display the cell above instead of running it, wrap it in a fence with
*more backticks* than the cell uses:

`````markdown
````markdown
```{r}
sum(1:10)
```
````
`````

which renders as:

````markdown
```{r}
sum(1:10)
```
````

The braces stay single. Nothing about the inner cell changes — it is shown
exactly as an author would type it, which is the point: a reader can copy it
straight into their own document.

### The outer fence must be longer

Markdown decides where a fenced code block ends by matching the length of its
opening fence. So the wrapping fence only needs to be *longer* than the
longest run of backticks inside it — one backtick longer is enough. A cell
written with the ordinary three backticks is displayed by wrapping it in four;
if the content being displayed already contains a four-backtick fence, wrap
that in five, and so on.

### Cell options are displayed too

Options on the fence header, and Quarto's `#|` comment options, are part of
the cell and are displayed along with it — nothing needs to be stripped or
adjusted. A fence-header option:

````markdown
```{r, echo=FALSE}
plot(1:10)
```
````

and a `#|` comment option:

````markdown
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-example
plot(1:10)
```
````

### Displaying a block that itself displays a cell

The same rule applies at any depth: each layer's fence just needs to be
longer than the longest fence nested inside it. To show a document like this
page — one that itself displays a cell — add one more layer of backticks:

``````markdown
`````markdown
````markdown
```{python}
1 + 1
```
````
`````
``````

::: callout-note
## Migrating from Quarto 1

Quarto 1 used doubled curly braces for this — a cell written as
`{{python}}` was displayed, with single braces, instead of running.
Quarto 2 does not support this escape: doubled braces in a fence
header produce a warning ([`Q-2-50`](../../errors/markdown/Q-2-50.qmd)),
and the fix is the `markdown` code block shown above. Dropping the
escape also means code blocks that genuinely contain doubled braces —
Jinja or Mustache templates, GitHub Actions expressions — render
correctly, where Quarto 1 would collapse them.
:::

## Cell openers

A code cell starts with a fence whose header is a single **language token**
in braces:

````markdown
```{python}
1 + 1
```
````

The token is letters, digits, `_`, `.` and `-`, starts with a letter, and is
matched case-insensitively. A dot is part of the token: `{python.marimo}` is
one token, naming a language and the engine flavor together. A space starts a
class instead: `{python .marimo}` is a `python` cell with the class `marimo`.

Options never go inside the braces. Put them in `#|` lines at the top of the
cell:

````markdown
```{python}
#| echo: false
1 + 1
```
````

A header such as `{python echo=false}` is the knitr style and is rejected
with error [`Q-2-36`](../../errors/markdown/Q-2-36.qmd).

## Where a cell's output appears

By default, a cell shows its code first and all of its output after the code,
even when the cell prints between statements:

````markdown
```{julia}
println("first")
x = 1
println("second")
x + 1
```
````

The rendered cell has one code block, followed by the outputs `first`,
`second`, and `2`.

The `output-interleave` option changes that. Set it to `true` and the cell
alternates code and output in the order the statements ran: the code up to the
first `println`, its output, the next statement, and so on. Set it in a cell:

````markdown
```{julia}
#| output-interleave: true
println("first")
x = 1
println("second")
x + 1
```
````

or for the whole document, under `execute`:

```yaml
execute:
  output-interleave: true
```

A cell's own setting overrides the document's setting.

Engines differ in whether they interleave by default:

| Engine | Default | `output-interleave` |
|---|---|---|
| Knitr | Interleaves | `false` holds the output |
| Julia | Holds | `true` interleaves |
| Jupyter | Holds | No effect yet |

For knitr cells that interleave, the chunk options `results: hold` and
`fig.show: hold` still work. They hold only printed text or only plots, and
leave messages and warnings where they were produced. `output-interleave:
false` holds everything.

::: callout-note
## Migrating from Quarto 1

Quarto 1 interleaved knitr output and held Julia and Jupyter output. Quarto 2
keeps those defaults. The new option lets Julia cells interleave. It also lets
knitr cells hold all of their output, without choosing between `results: hold`
and `fig.show: hold`.
:::

## Inline expressions

A document can also compute a value **inline** --- inside a sentence, or
inside an attribute --- so that the result appears in place of the
expression. Quarto has two spellings for this, and they differ in how the
computed value is inserted.

The **brace spelling** mirrors the cell syntax and works across engines:

````markdown
The current release is `{r} release_version`.
````

The **classic spelling** is knitr's own, inherited from R Markdown, and
predates Quarto. It is available with the knitr engine only:

````markdown
The current release is `r release_version`.
````

### The two spellings insert the value differently

The brace spelling **escapes** Markdown's special characters in the value:
whatever the expression returns is shown as text, exactly as it came out. The
classic spelling inserts the value **as Markdown**, so formatting carried in
the value is interpreted.

With `notice` set to `**important**`:

| Written              | Renders as      |
|----------------------|-----------------|
| `` `{r} notice` ``   | `**important**` |
| `` `r notice` ``     | **important**   |

To opt the brace spelling into Markdown, wrap the value in knitr's `I()`:

````markdown
The notice is `{r} I(notice)`.
````

That makes the two spellings equivalent: `` `r x` `` does the same thing as
`` `{r} I(x)` ``.

Reach for the brace spelling when the value comes from somewhere you do not
control. Markdown admits inline HTML, so a value inserted as Markdown can
bring markup with it; the brace spelling's escaping is the default for
exactly that reason.

### Where inline expressions work

Inline expressions are evaluated in three places: prose, attribute values
(a fenced div's attributes, or a link title), and the document's **own**
front matter:

````markdown
The current release is `{r} release_version`.

::: {#hero data-version="`{r} release_version`"}
Download the latest build.
:::

[Download](https://example.com/dl "Version `{r} release_version`")
````

In front matter, write the expression inside a quoted string:

````markdown
---
title: "Report for `{python} __import__('datetime').date.today().year`"
jupyter: python3
---
````

Front matter is evaluated before any cell runs, so a span there cannot use
variables a cell defines. A value that would put a newline inside a YAML
string stops the render and names the key.

They are left exactly as written in these places:

- any fenced code block, whether braced (a `{r}` cell) or not, and whatever
  its language;
- HTML comments;
- project-level metadata: `_quarto.yml`, `_metadata.yml`, and extension or
  format defaults. A span in `_quarto.yml` is **not** evaluated, even though
  one in a document's own front matter is;
- a span written in a language no engine in the document owns, such as
  `` `{zzz} x` ``.

::: callout-note
## Migrating from Quarto 1

Quarto 1 also evaluated a span written inside a braced `{r}` cell (a comment
such as `# a `{python} x` span`). Quarto 2 treats the cell body as code and
leaves it alone.
:::

### Inline expressions with Jupyter

With the [Jupyter engine](engines.qmd), a `` `{python} expr` `` span runs in
the document's kernel, so it sees the state left by earlier cells. The
language token matches case-insensitively: `{Python}` also runs in Quarto 2,
though Quarto 1 does not recognize it.

````markdown
```{python}
total = 40 + 2
```

The answer is `{python} total`.
````

The span is an **expression**, as in Quarto 1. A statement such as `y = 5`
has no value; the kernel answers with a `SyntaxError` and the render stops
with error [`Q-18-10`](../../errors/engine/Q-18-10.qmd), naming the span as
`file:line:col` together with the kernel's message. `error: true` does not
apply to a span, and neither does `execute: eval: false`: a span runs
either way.

#### How a value is inserted

As with knitr's brace spelling, the value is inserted as **text**, with
Markdown's special characters escaped. To insert Markdown (or HTML) instead,
return it from `IPython.display`:

````markdown
```{python}
from IPython.display import Markdown
note = Markdown("**important**")
```

The notice is `{python} note`.
````

`Markdown(...)` is the Jupyter analog of knitr's `I()`.

Two values need a word:

- `None` renders the text `None`, because that is the value's text.
- An empty string, or any value with no text form Quarto can place in the
  page (for example only a plot), leaves the span's source in the document.
  The second case also prints a warning naming the file and line; the render
  still succeeds.

::: callout-warning
## Empty values differ by engine

An empty string leaves the span source in place with Jupyter, while knitr and
Julia render nothing. This is not settled, so do not rely on either behavior
across engines.
:::

### Documents that contain only inline expressions

A document with no executable cell has no code for Quarto to hand to an
engine, so it needs a hint. Without one, its spans are left as written and no
kernel starts. Select the engine in the document's **own** front matter:

````markdown
---
title: Spans only
jupyter: python3
---

Today is `{python} __import__("datetime").date.today().year`.
````

`engine: jupyter` works too. The key must be in the document's own front
matter: `engine:` in `_quarto.yml` does not make a page without cells run its
spans, as in Quarto 1. A page with at least one executable cell needs no key.

To show a span as code instead of running it, wrap it in a `markdown` code
block, as in
[Writing about an inline expression](#writing-about-an-inline-expression).
Doubling the braces is not an escape: `` `{{python}} x` `` is left alone, but
it is displayed with both pairs of braces.

### Other engines

- **knitr**: unchanged. Both spellings work as described above.
- **Julia**: spans use the brace spelling, and Julia evaluates them. It finds
  spans by parsing the document as Markdown rather than scanning its text, so
  a couple of cases come out differently from Jupyter:
  - A span in the document's own front matter is left as written. Julia does
    not evaluate front matter spans.
  - The language and the code must be separated by one space. A tab leaves the
    span as written.

  As in any document, a span in a language that no engine in the document
  owns is left as written.
- **marimo**: inline expressions are not supported. marimo runs no spans, so
  a `` `{python} x` `` span in a marimo document is left as written, with no
  output. Compute the value in a cell and show it there.

### Writing about an inline expression

The rule is the one from [Displaying code cells without running
them](#displaying-code-cells-without-running-them), and nothing about it
changes for inline expressions: write it inside a `markdown` block and it is
displayed rather than run.

````markdown
```markdown
The current release is `{r} release_version`.
```
````

which renders as:

```markdown
The current release is `{r} release_version`.
```

The expression is shown exactly as an author would type it, together with the
prose around it, so a reader can copy the whole line into their own document.
As with cells, the wrapping fence only needs to be longer than the longest run
of backticks inside it.

Any fenced code block displays its text and never evaluates it, so the same
holds for a block with no language, or one labelled with another language such
as ```` ```r ```` or ```` ```text ````. A braced `{r}` cell is code, not
prose, and is not scanned for spans at all. Reach
for `markdown` when what you are showing is Quarto syntax, because that is the
label that tells readers (and highlighters) what the block contains.

::: callout-note
## Migrating from Quarto 1

Quarto 1 had a doubled-brace escape for inline expressions too: `` `{{r}} x` ``
was displayed as `` `{r} x` ``. Quarto 2 drops it for the same reason it drops
the doubled-brace escape for cells --- the `markdown` code block above does the
job, and leaving doubled braces alone is what lets Jinja and Mustache templates
render correctly.
:::
